analysis.one_liner: Requires insurance to cover at least 48 hospital hours after a mastectomy and 24 after lymph node surgery.
analysis.headline: Sponsored by Sen. Mary Landrieu with 11 Democratic cosponsors, the bill was referred to the Senate health committee on the day it was introduced in September 2003 and died there without a hearing or vote when the 108th Congress ended in January 2005.
analysis.plain_summary: Health insurers and employer plans could no longer cap covered hospital stays below 48 hours after a mastectomy or 24 hours after lymph node surgery for breast cancer, and could not require a doctor to get the plan's permission for the stay. A woman and her doctor could still choose for her to go home earlier [S3]. The bill also barred insurers from paying women rebates to skip the hospital, from dropping or refusing coverage to dodge the rule, and from penalizing doctors who followed it [S2][S3]. States with equal or stronger laws kept their own rules, and the requirements would have taken effect for plan years starting in 2004 [S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Women facing breast cancer surgery and their families: insurance would have to cover at least two nights in the hospital after a mastectomy, or one after lymph node removal, unless the woman and her doctor chose an earlier discharge [S3]. The bill also protected doctors from reimbursement cuts for keeping patients the full time [S2].

how_it_helps.text: Guarantees insurance coverage for at least 48 hours of hospital stay after a mastectomy and at least 24 hours after a lymph node dissection for breast cancer treatment.

Bars plans from making a provider get the insurer's authorization before prescribing that length of stay; an earlier discharge is allowed only when the attending provider decides in consultation with the patient.
Prohibits insurers from offering women payments or rebates to accept less than the minimum protections — the early-discharge rebate practice that drew 'drive-through mastectomy' criticism.
Bars plans from denying eligibility, enrollment, or renewal to avoid the requirements, and from penalizing or rewarding providers for shortening care.
Applies the same rules to individual-market insurance, and lets states that already require equal or stronger protections keep governing under their own laws.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and the employers who fund group plans, including self-insured employers covered through ERISA, would bear the added cost of longer covered stays, likely passed on through premiums. Patients could still owe deductibles and coinsurance, which the bill left in place, though cost-sharing could not increase during the required stay [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Health insurers and employer health plans

drawbacks.text: Guaranteed longer covered stays raise plan costs, which flow into premiums paid by employers and workers.
Plans keep deductibles and coinsurance, so patients can still face out-of-pocket costs for the mandated stay, although cost-sharing cannot rise during it.
It is not an absolute guarantee of two nights: a doctor, in consultation with the patient, can still send her home before the minimum stay ends.
It layers a federal benefit mandate on top of state insurance regulation, setting a federal floor only in states that have not passed an equal law of their own.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protection is real for women in states without their own law: two covered hospital nights after major cancer surgery instead of a stay an insurer could cap shorter, plus a ban on cash rebates to leave early. The cost is modest and spread widely — somewhat higher premiums across everyone with coverage — and insurers keep their deductibles, coinsurance, and freedom to negotiate provider payment rates [S3]. Because the bill exempted states with equal laws, its practical reach was limited to holdout states [S3].

outcome.mechanism: The Senate's health committee received the bill the day it was introduced and never held a hearing, markup, or vote; it died there when the 108th Congress ended in January 2005.

narrative.text: Sen. Mary Landrieu introduced the bill on September 30, 2003, joined by original cosponsors Sen. Patty Murray and Sen. Jon Corzine.
The Senate read the bill twice the same day and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
No further action was ever recorded — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — and the bill died when the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005.
All 11 cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican ever signed on, so the bill never built the support that might have forced committee action.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and employer-funded health plans kept the ability to cap and manage hospital stays after breast cancer surgery without a federal minimum, avoiding added benefit costs. Hospitals forwent the extra covered days, and women in states without their own mastectomy-stay law gained nothing.

against.name: Health insurance industry groups
against.what_they_did: Generally opposed new federal health coverage mandates during this era; this bill would have imposed one on group and individual coverage. No recorded action on this specific bill.

sides.party_line_note: Every Senate backer — the sponsor and all 11 cosponsors — was a Democrat, 12 of the chamber's 48 Democrats; no Republican cosponsored, and the Republican-chaired committee never acted, so the full Senate never voted.

industries.industry: Health insurers and group health plans
industries.note: The bill would have barred capping covered mastectomy stays below 48 hours, barred requiring the insurer's sign-off on a doctor-prescribed stay, and banned rebates to women who skip the hospital — removing the main cost-control levers on length of stay. Those costs would flow into premiums.
ERISA plans are covered, so employers who fund their own health plans would have paid for longer covered stays, while their employees gained the guarantee.
A guaranteed covered minimum stay means hospitals get paid for the 48 post-surgical hours that insurers could otherwise cut off.
The bill barred plans from cutting a doctor's reimbursement for following the minimum stay, and from offering incentives to discharge patients sooner.
